title: Dates of the events the Holy Days commemorate, as the sources give them
note: These are the historical events, not the yearly observances (for those, see years/<year>.json). Gregorian dates converted from Islamic lunar dates may differ by a day or two from the day actually reckoned, because Islamic months began with the sighting of the crescent. Source ids refer to https://lessan.github.io/bahai-date/sources.html.

events.time: 2 hours and 11 minutes after sunset on the evening of 22 May 1844, which began the day labelled 23 May
events.badi_date: 8 ‘Aẓamat 1 B.E. if Naw-Rúz 1844 was 20 March (the before-sunset rule); 7 ‘Aẓamat under the Western convention (Naw-Rúz on 21 March)
events.notes: “22 or 23 May” is a matter of labelling the evening, not a disagreement about the event (Lights of Guidance no. 1542).

gregorian_dates.note: The British consul in Tabríz, and Persian court historians

events.notes: The Dawn-Breakers says Sunday; 9 July 1850 was a Tuesday and 8 July a Monday (the court historian Sipihr gives Monday 27 Sha‘bán). With Naw-Rúz on 21 March 1850, 9 July was 16 Raḥmat and 17 Raḥmat was 10 July. The observance is fixed on 17 Raḥmat from 172 B.E.

God Passes By says “thirty-one days after Naw-Rúz”, which implies Naw-Rúz on 22 March 1863; the equinox fell before dawn on 21 March, which would make 22 April 14 Jalál. The festival is kept from 13 Jalál (Kitáb-i-Aqdas, Questions and Answers 1). The ninth and twelfth days of the event were 30 April and 3 May 1863.

gregorian_dates.note: The Bahá’í World volume 4; Nabíl’s account, whose Rúmí date (16 Ayyár) and count of seventy days from a Naw-Rúz on 20 March both point to 28 May

events.badi_date: 13 ‘Aẓamat, the seventieth day of the year, in every reckoning
events.notes: The Universal House of Justice named the day of the Ascension as one of the historical discrepancies it set aside (letter of 20 December 2017).
